nameStory: The 'jugularis' in this snail's scientific name comes from the Latin word for 'throat' or 'neck,' referring to the distinctive shape of its shell opening. Great pond snails get their common name from their preference for larger bodies of water and their impressive size compared to other freshwater snails. They're the gentle giants of New England's pond world!
description: Great pond snails are large freshwater snails with tall, spiral shells that can reach up to 2 inches in length. Their shells are typically brown to amber-colored with a glossy surface when wet, and they have a distinctive pointed spire that spirals upward. These air-breathing aquatic snails glide gracefully along underwater surfaces on their muscular foot, occasionally rising to the surface to breathe. You'll often see their long, tentacle-like eyestalks poking out as they explore their watery world.

idTips.label: Shell shape and size
idTips.description: Look for a large, tower-like shell up to 2 inches tall with 6-7 whorls spiraling to a sharp point - much larger than most pond snails you'll encounter

idTips.label: Shell opening
idTips.description: The shell opening (aperture) is oval-shaped and takes up about half the shell's total height, with a smooth, thin lip that feels delicate to the touch

idTips.label: Color and texture
idTips.description: Shell ranges from amber to dark brown with a glossy, almost glass-like surface when wet that becomes duller when dry

idTips.label: Body and tentacles
idTips.description: The soft body is grayish-brown with two triangular tentacles that have eyes at their base - much shorter and wider than the thread-like tentacles of smaller pond snails

idTips.label: Movement pattern
idTips.description: Glides smoothly along surfaces leaving a visible slime trail, and frequently rises to the water surface to breathe air through a visible breathing pore

habitat: Great pond snails prefer larger, permanent bodies of water like ponds, slow-moving streams, and quiet backwaters of rivers throughout New England. They thrive in areas with abundant aquatic vegetation and soft, muddy bottoms where they can find decaying plant matter to eat. Look for them in waters that don't freeze completely in winter and have good oxygen levels.

seasonality.spring: Active snails emerge from winter dormancy and begin feeding actively. This is when you're most likely to spot them gliding along pond edges as they search for fresh algae and plant matter.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when snails are most visible. They're often seen at the water surface breathing air, especially during warm afternoons when oxygen levels in the water may be lower.
seasonality.fall: Snails prepare for winter by feeding heavily and may be found deeper in the water. Empty shells often wash up on shores as some individuals complete their life cycle.
seasonality.winter: Most snails retreat to deeper water or bury in mud to survive freezing. Activity is minimal, though they may occasionally be seen in areas that remain unfrozen.

funFact: Great pond snails are actually lung-breathing animals that evolved from land snails and returned to water - they still need to surface regularly to breathe air through a special breathing hole, making them some of the only 'scuba diving' snails in New England!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other large pond snails, but Great pond snails are noticeably larger with a more elongated, tower-like shell compared to the rounder shells of smaller species. Memory trick: 'Great' means big and tall - if it's smaller than your thumb or looks squat, it's probably a different species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'pond' snails, these creatures are actually more closely related to land snails than to marine snails, which explains why they breathe air instead of extracting oxygen from water like fish. This air-breathing adaptation can be confusing to observers who expect all aquatic animals to have gills.
compareHints: **Note: Identification uncertain due to limited reference material** Within the Lymnaeidae family, Great pond snails are distinguished by their large size and tall, pointed shells compared to other pond snails which tend to be smaller and more rounded. The elongated shell shape and substantial size make them relatively easy to distinguish from other freshwater snails in New England waters.
